interactions.label: A casualty doctor examines an assault victim's injuries and issues a wound certi

params.question: A casualty doctor examines an assault victim's injuries and issues a wound certificate. In which medicolegal capacity is the doctor operating?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The expert witness capacity involves testifying in court about medical findings — it is not engaged when examining patients in casualty.
Correct. When examining living patients with legal implications and issuing wound certificates, the doctor operates as a clinical examiner under BNSS 2023 provisions.
The autopsy surgeon capacity involves post-mortem examination of deceased persons, not the examination of living patients.
State medicine deals with community health and vital statistics — it does not involve individual patient examination for legal purposes.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the three capacities: clinical examiner (living patients, wound certificates under BNSS), autopsy surgeon (deceased, post-mortem reports), and expert witness (court testimony under BSA).
The doctor's three medicolegal capacities — clinical examiner, autopsy surgeon, and expert witness — are each governed by a different body of law and produce distinct documentation.

interactions.label: Which statement correctly distinguishes a Police Inquest from a Magistrate's Inq

params.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a Police Inquest from a Magistrate's Inquest under BNSS 2023?

answers.text: Both types carry the same legal weight and impose identical obligations on the doctor

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The two types differ in legal weight — a Magistrate's Inquest carries greater formal authority and imposes different obligations on the attending doctor.

answers.text: A Police Inquest is triggered only for natural deaths occurring at home

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A Police Inquest under BNSS Section 194 is triggered by sudden, unnatural, suspicious, or violent deaths — not by natural deaths.

answers.text: A Police Inquest is conducted by the investigating officer under BNSS Section 194

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The fundamental distinction is who conducts the inquiry: the investigating officer (Police Inquest, BNSS Section 194) versus a judicial magistrate (Magistrate's Inquest), each triggered by different circumstances.

answers.text: Only the Magistrate's Inquest requires the presence of a medical doctor

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both types of inquest may involve the doctor as an examiner and/or witness, though the nature and extent of the doctor's formal obligations differ.

overallFeedback.feedback: The two inquest types differ in who conducts them (police officer vs magistrate), the circumstances that trigger them, their legal weight, and the doctor's formal obligations at each.

The Police Inquest (BNSS Section 194, formerly CrPC Section 174) is conducted by the investigating officer for sudden or suspicious deaths. The Magistrate's Inquest is a judicial proceeding carrying greater formal authority.

interactions.label: MCCD Form 4A is used for deaths occurring in the community, while Form 4 is used

params.question: MCCD Form 4A is used for deaths occurring in the community, while Form 4 is used for hospital deaths.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: The forms are reversed in this statement. Form 4 is issued for deaths occurring outside a hospital — at home or in the community. Form 4A is specifically for deaths within a registered medical institution.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Well identified. It is the reverse: Form 4 is for deaths outside hospitals (community, home, non-institutional settings), completed by the attending physician. Form 4A is for deaths within a registered medical institution.

interactions.label: A severely burned woman in the emergency department tells the attending doctor,

params.question: A severely burned woman in the emergency department tells the attending doctor, 'I know I am dying — my mother-in-law poured kerosene on me.' She is conscious and coherent. What is the doctor's MOST important immediate medicolegal duty regarding this statement?

answers.text: Record only a brief summary of the accusation in the case sheet

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A summary is legally insufficient. The dying declaration must be recorded verbatim in the patient's own words, or it may be challenged as inaccurate and rendered inadmissible.

answers.text: Advise the patient to conserve strength and make a formal statement to the police later

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A dying patient may not survive to make a later statement. Delaying risks losing irreplaceable evidence and breaches the doctor's medicolegal duty to record the declaration when it is made.

answers.text: Record the statement verbatim, documenting her mental state and belief that death is imminent

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The doctor must record the statement in the patient's own words and document that she is conscious, coherent, and believes death is imminent. Any deficiency in recording or attestation can render the declaration inadmissible.

answers.text: Decline to record the statement because only a Magistrate can take a valid dying declaration

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A dying declaration can be validly recorded by any person present, including the attending doctor. Waiting for a magistrate risks losing the statement entirely if the patient dies.

overallFeedback.feedback: When a patient who believes death is imminent makes a statement, the attending doctor must record it verbatim, noting the patient's mental state and belief of imminent death. This duty cannot be deferred — any recording deficiency may render the statement inadmissible in court.

A dying declaration recorded by the attending doctor is legally valid, provided the patient's mental fitness, expressed belief of imminent death, and verbatim statement are all documented. The principle nemo moriturus praesumitur mentire presumes a dying person has no reason to lie.
